chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from one of his companions, from Ibn Abi Hamza, who said:

I heard Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) saying to his son: 'O my son! Whoever from you is struck by a calamity or an affliction descends upon him, let him perform ablution and perfect the ablution, then let him pray two or four cycles of prayer, then let him say at the end of these:'

'O the Place of every complaint, and O the Listener of every whisper, and Witness of every gathering, and Knower of every secret, and O the Repeller of whatever He wills from affliction, and O the Friend of Ibrahim, and O the Whisperer to Musa, and O the Chosen One of Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family)! I supplicate to You with the supplication of one whose destitution is severe, whose plan is scarce, and whose strength has weakened. The supplication of the drowning, the stranger, the desperate one who finds no one to remove what he is in except You, O the Most Merciful of the merciful.'
For indeed, whoever supplicates with it, Allah will remove [the affliction] from him, if Allah wills.
ai.seo_question: What is the ritual and supplication for removing calamity and distress in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: Recorded in Al-Kafi, this tradition from Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin) outlines a specific ritual for averting calamities, emphasizing the spiritual efficacy of combining ritual purity (wudu) with voluntary prayer (salat al-hajah). The supplication highlights Allah as the ultimate refuge for the distressed, reflecting the Shia emphasis on divine mercy and the intercessory power of sincere invocation during times of grief or fear.
